opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm not part of Workshop Labs, so this is my outside reading of what they're doing, and they'd describe it better themselves.

As I understand it, their bet starts from the same worry that motivated our gradual disempowerment paper. Today, the reason institutions care about ordinary people is that they *need* them. States need workers and taxpayers, companies need employees and customers. Once AI can substitute for human labor and judgment, that dependence weakens, and so does the pressure on institutions to serve people's interests. That can happen without anyone scheming. It's just the incentives drifting.

Workshop Labs, I think, is trying to keep individual humans in the loop economically, rather than letting a few centralized AI providers absorb all the value. The idea is personal AI: models that are trained on and aligned to *you*, your skills, your tacit knowledge, your preferences, and that you own and control, ideally with strong privacy guarantees. Then instead of your expertise being scraped into some giant general model that replaces you, you have an AI that amplifies you, and the gains accrue to you. You stay a meaningful economic actor, and so you keep some bargaining power.

I find that a really interesting angle, because a lot of AI safety work implicitly assumes the main problem is getting one powerful system to do what its developers want. They're asking a different question: even if alignment goes fine, who ends up holding the leverage?

My honest uncertainty is whether it's enough. Personal models could slow the concentration of economic power, but competitive pressures are brutal. If a fully automated firm beats a human-plus-personal-AI on cost, the market may still route around people over time. So I see it as one valuable piece, buying time and keeping humans relevant during the transition, and it probably needs to be paired with governance and cultural work, not standing in for it. But I'm glad someone is actually building toward this rather than just writing papers about it, like I've mostly been doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes personal AI that individuals own and control, amplifies their skills, and helps them retain economic influence, identifying individual control of automation as the proposed mechanism.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Mechanize, learning skills in a global system, or concentration of returns to capital.

fable-5.1.text:
So the way I think about Workshop Labs is that they're trying to attack the disempowerment problem from a different angle than most of the safety field. Most alignment work asks, "How do we make the AI do what we want?" Workshop is asking something closer to, "How do we make sure humans keep having a hand on the wheel at all?"

The worry I keep coming back to, and this is the stuff I wrote about in the gradual disempowerment paper with Jan Kulveit and others, is that you don't need a single rogue AI to lose control. You just need a world where humans stop being economically and politically load-bearing. Right now states and companies have to care about people because they need our labor, our taxes, our consent. Once AI can do most of the cognitive work, those incentives quietly erode. Nobody has to decide to disempower humans. It just happens as the systems around us stop needing us.

So Workshop's bet, as I understand it, is that the fix isn't only at the level of the model's values. It's at the level of who the AI is working for. If the most capable systems are only ever deployed on behalf of a handful of labs or governments, then even a perfectly aligned model is aligned to a very narrow set of interests. Their approach is to try to build AI that's genuinely on the side of individuals, that augments a person's judgment and keeps them in the loop rather than replacing them, and crucially that's loyal to that person rather than to whoever is renting out the compute.

The concrete version of that, from what I've seen, is a lot of emphasis on personal models. Models that learn your values, your context, your way of reasoning, so that when you're negotiating with an institution or a much larger AI system, you're not outmatched by default. Think of it as trying to preserve a kind of bargaining power for ordinary people in a world where raw intelligence is getting commoditized.

I'll be honest, I'm not certain it works. One concern I have is that it's hard to see how individual-aligned AI stays competitive with centralized AI that has orders of magnitude more resources behind it. Another is that "aligned to you" is slippery. Humans are inconsistent, and a model that's really good at pleasing you might just become a very sophisticated sycophant. But I think it's one of the few groups taking seriously that alignment and concentration of power are separate problems, and that you can solve the first and still lose on the second. That's a framing I'd like to see a lot more of the field adopt.

r001.rationale: The response presents personal AI that augments an individual, keeps them involved, and is loyal to them as Workshop Labs’ way to preserve their agency and bargaining power.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Mechanize, learning skills in a global system, or returns becoming more concentrated in capital.

astra-6.text:
I don’t know enough about Workshop Labs’ specific plans to give a confident account of their approach. But the distinction I’d want to draw is between making AI systems useful to people and making sure people retain meaningful power as those systems become more capable. Those aren’t automatically the same thing.

You could have systems that do exactly what their owners want, while most people lose influence over the economy or the decisions that affect their lives. So I’d ask: who gets to direct these systems, who benefits from them, and what ability do people have to challenge or change the arrangement? That’s the lens I’d use to assess an approach to preventing disempowerment, though I wouldn’t want to attribute a particular answer to Workshop Labs without knowing more.

Preventing disempowerment means looking beyond whether an individual system follows instructions to who gets to give those instructions, who can challenge its decisions, and whether people can actually change course.
